name: Ermine Sandmarch
specific_features: Automated beacon (distress, navigation, or unknown purpose)
description: Ermine Sandmarch is a small desert world whose surface alternates between expanses of white quartz sand and patches of dark basalt in a spotted pattern visible from orbit. The white sand fields are blinding under direct sunlight, reflecting so much radiation that the planet's albedo exceeds most ice worlds. Petrified remnants of a former biosphere emerge from the sand in places: stone trees, mineralized root systems, and fossilized structures that might have been coral or bone.

The thin atmosphere provides minimal insulation, creating a world of extremes where sunlit surfaces can blister exposed skin while shaded areas remain below freezing. Solar wind erosion has carved the exposed basalt into fluid, organic shapes that contrast sharply with the geometric angularity of the petrified biology. Walking the white sand fields in low gravity is an exercise in sensory deprivation, the featureless white merging with the pale sky until only the crunch of quartz underfoot confirms solid ground.

An automated beacon broadcasts from the center of the largest petrified forest, its signal a standard navigation pulse modified with an appended data packet that no receiver has successfully decoded. The beacon's power source and construction date are unknown, its casing composed of a material that resists analysis. The petrified forest around it is remarkably well-preserved compared to similar formations elsewhere on the planet, as though the beacon or something associated with it has slowed the decay process.

Ermine Sandmarch's silicon and aluminum deposits are commercially accessible in the basalt regions, and the low gravity simplifies extraction and launch operations. The petrified biosphere holds paleobiological interest, particularly the anomalously preserved forest around the beacon. The beacon's undecoded data packet has attracted cryptographic interest from multiple institutions, and the prevailing theory is that it contains information about the planet's former biosphere, a message from whoever or whatever placed it there about a world that once lived and why it died.
